# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transfemoral arterial access remains the default route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore structural heart procedures, but it is unsuitable in a meaningful minority of patients. The transcaval (TCv) vascular approach is increasingly used in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in patients unsuitable for the gold-standard transfemoral approach. While the transfemoral approach is the preferred vascular access for TAVR, it may be unfeasible in approximately 5–10% of patients due to anatomical challenges such as small vessel size, marked vessel tortuosity or extensive calcification of the iliofemoral vasculature [1]. Transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous alternative that preserves the operator ergonomics of a retrograde transfemoral procedure [2].

## Concept and Pathophysiology

Caval-aortic access refers to percutaneous entry into the abdominal aorta from the femoral vein through the adjoining inferior vena cava [3]. The technique was first validated preclinically, demonstrating that large therapeutic devices can be introduced into the aorta via the IVC in a simple catheter procedure, and the fistula closed uneventfully despite full anticoagulation [4]. The counterintuitive safety of the approach rests on a hydraulic principle: although counterintuitive, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole [5].

## Technique

The procedure is enabled by transcatheter electrosurgery. Transcatheter electrosurgery refers to a family of procedures using radiofrequency energy to vaporize and traverse or lacerate tissue despite flowing blood; tissue traversal requires guidewire insulation and adjunctive insulating catheters to concentrate charge at the tip of traversing guidewires [6]. In practice, transcaval access is obtained over an electrified guidewire directed from the inferior vena cava toward a snare in the abdominal aorta; after delivering a microcatheter to exchange for a stiff guidewire, the transcatheter heart valve introducer sheath is advanced from the femoral vein into the abdominal aorta for conventional transfemoral retrograde TAVR; the aorto-caval access site is closed with a nitinol cardiac occluder [7].

## Pre-Procedural Planning

Computed tomography is central to candidate selection. Investigators have described how to isolate (segment) aortoiliac arteries and IVC and find a calcium-free "target window" (wider than the proposed introducer sheath) on the right wall of the aorta close to the IVC, because heavily calcific targets are difficult to cross and may increase the risk of complications [8]. A dedicated CT classification scheme grades anatomy from favourable to unfavourable for transcaval crossing [9].

## Clinical Evidence in TAVR

The first-in-human series described the first use of caval-aortic access and closure to enable transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in patients who lacked other access options [10]. This was followed by a prospective, independently adjudicated, multicentre trial in which 100 patients underwent attempted percutaneous transcaval access to the abdominal aorta by electrifying a caval guidewire and advancing it into a pre-positioned aortic snare; after exchanging for a rigid guidewire, conventional TAVR was performed through transcaval introducer sheaths [11]. The trial concluded that transcaval access enabled TAVR in patients who were not good candidates for transthoracic access, and bleeding and vascular complications, using permeable nitinol cardiac occluders to close the access ports, were common but acceptable in this high-risk cohort [11].

Twelve-month follow-up was reassuring: there were no late vascular complications of transcaval access; 93% of fistulas were proven occluded at last follow-up, and only one was proven patent after 12 months [12]. A multicentre European registry reported that transcaval access was successful in 49 out of 50 patients and device success was obtained in 94% of cases, and closure of the caval-aortic puncture site with a nitinol cardiac occluder was successful in all cases without need for emergent surgery [13].

Comparative data emerged from a propensity-weighted analysis of eight experienced centers that contributed local data collected for the STS/ACC TVT Registry between 2017 and 2020 [14]. In that analysis, stroke or TIA were significantly less common after transcaval as compared with transaxillary access before and after propensity weighting (2.5% vs 13.2%) [14], while bleeding and vascular complications were comparable between transcaval and transaxillary groups [14].

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies collectively including 467 patients [15] found that TCv-TAVR procedures achieved a success rate of 98.5% [15], with all-cause mortality of 6.4% after 30 days and 14.4% after one year [16], supporting the conclusion that transcaval TAVR is a reasonable option when transfemoral access is not feasible [17]. An earlier systematic review of transcaval access for endovascular aortic interventions reported that the overall technical success rate for all procedures is 96.2%, with a 4.3% mortality rate [18].

## Closure Devices

Closure has historically relied on off-label nitinol occluders, prompting development of purpose-built devices. Transcaval access enables delivery of large-caliber devices to the aorta in patients ineligible for transfemoral arterial access; closure of aorto-caval fistulae using off-label nitinol cardiac occluders has been shown to be safe, but persistent aorto-caval fistulae at exit from the catheterization lab and bleeding complications were common in a prospective study [19]. A dedicated transcaval closure device has since been evaluated in first-in-human testing [19], and best-practice guidance has been published to standardise technique [5].

## Beyond TAVR

The approach extends to other large-bore interventions. Transcaval access has been applied for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR), transcatheter mechanical circulatory support (MCS) to avoid limb ischemia, and interventional pediatric cardiology [5]. The first TEVAR application demonstrated that it was used in a 61-year-old man with a descending thoracic aneurysm, performed in lieu of a surgical iliac conduit in view of small atherosclerotic pelvic arteries [20]. For mechanical circulatory support, a series reported that all ten patients underwent emergency implantation of the 7 mm diameter Impella 5.0 device via transcaval access [21], concluding that transcaval access is feasible for emergency nonsurgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries [21]. Transcaval crossing is among many electrosurgical applications, alongside leaflet-laceration procedures such as BASILICA and LAMPOON [22].

## Conclusions

Transcaval access has matured from a preclinical concept into an established alternative for patients without good transfemoral options [23]. It is a feasible and safe alternative TAVI access strategy for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis not suitable for transfemoral and transaxillary/subclavian access, and outcomes are expected to improve as centres gain experience and a dedicated caval-aortic closure device becomes available [13]. Limitations of the current evidence include the absence of randomised data and reliance on specialised, high-volume centres [15]. Standardised planning, training, and dedicated closure technology are likely to further broaden safe adoption [24,25].
